content: Compared to flurbiprofen (50 mg), there is very low-certainty evidence regarding its effects. Maternal functioning, well-being, and experiences of postnatal care were not reported in the included trials. Similarly, newborn outcomes, breastfeeding status, and adverse effects were not reported. When comparing aspirin to ketorolac, it remains uncertain whether any dose of aspirin provides adequate pain relief for uterine cramping or involution as reported by women, compared to any dose of ketorolac. Subgroup analyses based on the dose of analgesic (ketorolac 5 mg or 10 mg) showed the same level of uncertainty. It is also uncertain whether aspirin affects the need for additional pain relief compared to ketorolac. Adverse effects of aspirin compared to ketorolac are similarly uncertain, with subgroup analyses showing consistent uncertainty. Newborn outcomes, breastfeeding status, and adverse effects were not reported in the included trials. When comparing codeine (60 mg) to nalbuphine (15 mg), it is uncertain whether codeine affects the need for additional pain relief. Relief of symptoms, maternal functioning, well-being, and postnatal care experiences were not reported. Similarly, newborn outcomes, breastfeeding status, and adverse effects were not reported. For paracetamol (650 mg) compared to NSAIDs (e.g., aspirin 650 mg), it is uncertain whether paracetamol provides adequate pain relief for uterine cramping or involution. Adverse effects of paracetamol compared to NSAIDs are also uncertain. Subgroup analyses based on type and dose of analgesic (e.g., paracetamol 650 mg vs. aspirin 650 mg or paracetamol 1000 mg vs. naproxen 500 mg) showed the same level of uncertainty. Maternal functioning, well-being, and postnatal care experiences were not reported. Similarly, newborn outcomes, breastfeeding status, and adverse effects were not reported. When comparing aspirin (650 mg) to codeine (60 mg or 120 mg), it is uncertain whether aspirin provides adequate pain relief for uterine cramping or involution. Subgroup analyses of various NSAIDs (e.g., flurbiprofen 50 mg, naproxen 300 mg or 600 mg, fenoprofen 200 mg) compared to codeine (60 mg or 120 mg) showed consistent uncertainty. Adverse effects of NSAIDs compared to opioids are also uncertain. Maternal functioning, well-being, and postnatal care experiences were not reported. Similarly, newborn outcomes, breastfeeding status, and adverse effects were not reported. For herbal analgesia compared to NSAIDs, it is uncertain whether mefenamic acid (250 mg) or ibuprofen (400 mg) provides adequate pain relief for uterine cramping or involution compared to herbal remedies (e.g., fennel essence, Melissa officinalis). Subgroup analyses showed consistent uncertainty. Adverse effects of NSAIDs compared to herbal analgesia are also uncertain. Maternal functioning, well-being, and postnatal care experiences were not reported. Similarly, newborn outcomes, breastfeeding status, and adverse effects were not reported. Regarding pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) for postpartum women, routine initiation of PFMT after childbirth is not recommended for the prevention of urinary or fecal incontinence. However, women experiencing urinary stress incontinence postpartum should be informed about the potential benefits of PFMT for treating urinary incontinence. Unsupervised pelvic floor exercises performed at home may be beneficial and are unlikely to cause harm. PFMT may also positively impact sexual function and promote self-care during the postnatal period. All women should be informed during pregnancy and postpartum about potential pelvic floor problems, including urinary or fecal incontinence. Evidence from 19 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 5452 women, mostly conducted in high-income countries, was reviewed. Trials included both preventive and therapeutic PFMT interventions. For women who were continent at enrollment, PFMT was intended as a preventive measure, while for those with incontinence symptoms, it was therapeutic. It remains uncertain whether PFMT affects urinary or fecal incontinence in the mid-postnatal period (3–6 months) or late postnatal period (>6–12 months) compared to usual care. Long-term effects on maternal morbidity and adverse effects were not reported. Postnatal care experiences were also not reported. Economic evaluations of pharmacological treatments for uterine cramping or involution pain relief were not identified. For PFMT programs with supervised components, group-based PFMT may be more cost-effective than individual sessions. However, PFMT may decrease equity due to limited service availability and potential out-of-pocket costs, particularly if provided by specialist personnel. Equity may improve if PFMT is delivered or supervised by midwives or nurses.
